utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Daniela Kravetz for the Prosecution, with my colleague Aditya Menon; our Case Manager, Line Pedersen; and our legal intern Thomas Dutton. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ben Emmerson for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rodney Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, Andrew Strong, and Kushtrim Zymberi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Emmerson. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, with Colleen Rohan, Chad Mair, and Mr. Gentian Zyberi is appearing pro bono today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Richard Harvey, assisted by Mr. Luke Boenisch and Rudina Jasini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey. Just before we begin, can I just ask a few questions, ma'am. We've got on the notification list from the Prosecution for this week both Witnesses 80 and -- or shall we go into private session? What I just want to find out is whether -- are these people coming, 80 and 75?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In relation to Witness 80, Your Honours, we have a motion pending before the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- to either proceed via videolink for the testimony of this witness or do a Rule 4 sitting. So we have listed him on the basis of that application that has been made to Your Honours. That's why he's listed as the last witness for the sitting period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I suggest we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Witness 77. We need to go into closed session to allow the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to sit closer to the microphone for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you please approach the microphone, sir. Just move --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe the usher could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, can I ask that the witness be given a pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to look at the document that's being handed to you or will be handed to you in a minute, and without reading it out loud I'm going to ask you to confirm whether the details on this document are correct. Could you please just read that to yourself and let me know if the details -- if your personal details indicated in that document are correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the pseudonym sheet, that's Exhibit 03100, and I seek to tender that under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 03100 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it shall be assigned Exhibit P301.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, when did the FARK forces enter Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime in 1998. It was the beginning of June, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And could you tell us, if you know, the size of the FARK forces that entered Kosovo in -- on the date that you have indicated? By that I mean how many men approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 134 Brigade had about 200, 250 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what type of weaponry these forces brought into Kosovo, if any, when they entered in the date that you have indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Light armament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Automatic rifles, rifles, grenades, hand-grenades.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did these FARK forces have any type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did have camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what was the purpose of these forces, the FARK forces, entering Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The aim of the FARK forces was to fight Serb paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who decided that these forces would enter Kosovo in the period you have indicated, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision was taken by Ahmet Krasniqi, because the General Staff was in Tirana, and Colonel Tahir Zemaj was tasked with this entry and Ahmet Krasniqi was the one who gave the order for the forces to enter Kosovo as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You have mentioned a couple of names. I just want to clarify who these persons are for the Court. Could you tell us first who is -- who was Ahmet Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahmet Krasniqi was the commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where was he based at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You also referred to a person by the name of Colonel Tahir Zemaj. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 134 Brigade. He was appointed by Ahmet Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did Tahir Zemaj enter Kosovo along with the 134th Brigade that you've referred to in June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the leader of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know whether these FARK forces, once they entered Kosovo, do you know if they went to any particular village within Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially they stopped at Jasiq village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And for how long did they, these forces, remain at Jasiq village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several days. I can't remember how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know whether, after the arrival of the FARK forces in Kosovo, did Tahir Zemaj have any meetings with Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they met. There was a meeting in Junik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when that meeting in Junik took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about two or three days after the 134th Brigade got to Jasiq. This meeting was scheduled then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who organised the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Naim Maloku and another person, I can't remember this person's name, and the commander in Junik. I can't remember his name either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's okay. You've referred to a person by the name of Naim Maloku. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an officer. It was said at the time that he had been an officer in the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose was that the forces wanted to continue on their way to go to an interior part of Kosovo in the Decani area. And they met the resistance of some people and they couldn't go on from Jasiq to the vicinity of Decan, in one of the villages near Decan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that answer, sir. You say "the purpose was that the forces wanted to continue on their way ..." Which forces are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 134th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say "they met the resistance of some people and they couldn't go on from Jasiq," which people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramush Haradinaj had sent word that they shouldn't dare to enter further in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify, sir. When you say he "had sent word that they shouldn't dare to enter further," who are you referring to by "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same brigade, the 134th Brigade that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Oh, I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's fine to interrupt at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, before the break you had told us that while this 134th Brigade was in Jasiq, Ramush Haradinaj had sent word that they should not dare to enter further into Kosovo. How do you know this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tahir Zemaj, the commander, told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know who came on behalf of Ramush Haradinaj to convey that message to the FARK forces in Jasiq?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Naim Maloku and it was for that reason that the meeting was scheduled to be held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did Ramush Haradinaj attend this meeting that was organised in Junik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know if he came alone or did he come with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was accompanied by the military police. This is how they were called at the time. But I don't know who exactly was together with him. However, I know that Naim Maloku was there and a couple of other officers, but I don't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these persons that you describe as military police, did they wear any type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did this uniform have any sort of insignia or badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The KLA one. But I can't remember whether it was PU-KLA or not. But the black uniforms were of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think you said you can't remember if it was PU-KLA or not. What does PU stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know what was discussed during this meeting which Ramush Haradinaj attended in Junik?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, before the witness answers, could Ms. Kravetz please lay the foundation for knowledge before the witness testifies. In other words, was he present at the meeting, what is the source of his information. That's going to become a theme of objections if questions are asked in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sure, no problem, I can back up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us with whom Mr. Haradinaj met when he went to Junik on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Same objection, same reasons, please, basis of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I believe the witness will tell us whether he knows that or not and I can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, do you know with whom Mr. Haradinaj met when he went to Junik on this occasion that you've been describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He met Tahir Zemaj, Nazif Ramabaja, and another officer whose name I can't remember; however, I was not in the room where the meeting was held. I was in the ante-room with some other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you see Ramush Haradinaj on that occasion in Junik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And had you met him or encountered him before that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was the first time that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did you know that the person you saw was Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who knew him said that this was Ramush Haradinaj, this person was Naim Maloku, and I don't remember the name of the third person. I think he was commander in Junik, but I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine. You've told us that you did not attend the meeting; you were in the ante-room with other soldiers. Did any of the persons who attended the meeting tell you what was discussed during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. After people came out of the meeting, Tahir Zemaj told us all that there were some problems, that orders had been given for us to go back to Albania and not enter further into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify that answer, sir. When you say that he told you all that there were some problems, what exactly did he say? What sort of problems are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem was that these officers could not get further into mainland Kosovo because they were not welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "these officers could not get further into ... Kosovo," whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tahir Zemaj was commander of 134th Brigade, but there were other officers, 25 of them, who had served in the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us earlier that orders had been given for you to go back to Albania and not to enter further into Kosovo. Who gave those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that Tahir said that Ramush, Naim Maloku, and the other person said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say that these officers, that is, Tahir Zemaj and the other officers, were not welcome, whom are you referring to when you say they were not welcome? By whom were they not welcome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, in the meeting there were three people, Ramush, Naim Maloku, and the third person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you completed your answer, sir? I was asking: Who did not welcome Tahir Zemaj and the other officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramush, Naim Maloku, and the third person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I think now it's clear. As a result of this meeting between Ramush Haradinaj, Tahir Zemaj, and the other officers you've referred to, did the FARK forces leave the village of Jasiq?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did they remain in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about ten days, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And after those ten days, where did these forces go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They remained there until Sali Ceku, Ismet Ceku [as interpreted], and myself --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I stop you there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe we should go into private session for this portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we please go into closed session so the witness can be brought back in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, did you see Ramush Haradinaj again after the incident that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the next time you saw him after this incident, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next time after this incident was when he came, because we were billeted in Prapaqan, in a school, the entire 134th Brigade was stationed there with all its officers. One day Ramush and Toger came there. They entered the premises of the school. There were guards there, guarding that barracks, as we called it then, and Haradinaj and Toger entered the yard of the school and demanded that that facility be vacated within 20 or 30 minutes, I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had told us earlier that the 134th Brigade was billeted in the village of Isniq. Do you recall when the brigade moved to the village of Prapaqan, to that school you've referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some days, I was still recovering. After I recovered, when I came there, I saw that they were stationed in the school in Prapaqan. Maybe two or three weeks, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said when -- referring to when Ramush and Toger came to the premises of the school, you said that they entered the school-yard and demanded that the facility be vacated. Who did they speak to and say this to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know initially who they spoke to. But when they fired in the air, everybody came out. And then what was -- to see what was happening. And Ramush and Toger were there together with some other soldiers dressed in black clothes. That improvised barracks had -- was full of soldiers in black clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say that they fired in the air and everybody came out, whom are you referring to? Who fired in the air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody. The officers, the soldiers came out to see what was happening, because part of the brigade was -- were drilling. Some others were inside the school. Tahir Zemaj too came out to see and asked what the problem was, and then he was told that: You must free the school and go to where you came from. These were the words that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was asking who was firing. I understand who went out to see what was happening, but who was firing in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did Tahir Zemaj re --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how did Tahir Zemaj respond when Ramush Haradinaj said these words to him, You must free the school and go to where you came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said this is not good. We shouldn't engage in fratricide. We will vacate this facility. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did that happen? Did the 134th Brigade vacate the school in Prapaqan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All the officers packed their bags and vacated the barracks, but they wanted to leave the soldiers there. Ramush and Rrustem Tetaj started to talk in front of the army and they -- I was present there, and they said that: This is the hand of Serbia. They have come from Serbia. Don't listen to them. At those moments, all the soldiers threw down their weapons -- their weapons and wanted to leave the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did the soldiers leave the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment they didn't do so immediately, but they dropped their weapons on the ground. They didn't agree, of course, with what was being told them -- to them to do, to free the barracks. We went again to this house in Isniq, to this guest-room. This didn't last -- this incident didn't last long.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did the 134th Brigade eventually leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Because in the evening Rrustem Tetaj talked with Tahir Zemaj. They decided to have a meeting in Lluke e Poshtme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You've referred to a person by the name of Rrustem Tetaj. Could you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He acted as a commander in Lluke e Poshtme staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just for the record could you again tell us the name of the village where they decided to have a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my recollection it was called Lluke e Poshtme, where Rrustem Tetaj was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know what happened during this meeting in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't be precise, but I know that an agreement was reached and that everyone turned back to the school of Prapaqan, to that improvised barracks that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I know you've said you can't be precise, but do you know what sort of agreement was reached? And if you don't know, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I told you that I only know that all officers returned to the barracks and that's it. I don't know any more about the agreement because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Sir, during your testimony today you have referred to Toger, and I asked you earlier what was his full name and you said that that was Idriz Balaj. Can you tell us when you first became aware that this person whom you knew by the name of Toger was called, in fact, Idriz Balaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely when and how I learned that it was Idriz Balaj. I only recall that people were saying that he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this time. The witness has answered the question: "I can't remember precisely when and how I learned that it was Idriz Balaj," which is the answer to Ms. Kravetz's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's fine. I can continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, based on the information you had at the time - and I'm speaking about 1998 - what kind of reputation did this person you knew as Toger have at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- I'm going to -- I'm going to object to that question on series of grounds, not the least of which is relevance. It's also prejudice outweighs the probative value. Also I believe under Rule 93 it's an impermissible question. And once again it goes to the very thing that I started this trial with, which is issues concerning rumour are inappropriate and Mr. Balaj's reputation is not an issue in this case. And I trust the Prosecution does not attempt to seek a conviction based on reputation, especially reputation based on rumour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness about his personal knowledge based on the information he had at the time, and he can respond whether he had any information or did not have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was not the question posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I simply say this: If Ms. Kravetz wishes to adduce evidence of reputation, she would need first to identify to what issue that goes, in other words, to what is its relevance said to be judged against. But if it's simply suggested that evidence of reputation is going to assist this Trial Chamber in considerations of the merits of the proceedings, then, in our submission, that would plainly be an unarguable position. So before evidence of reputation, particularly generalised information of this kind, is adduced, as a very minimum Ms. Kravetz must specify as to what the issue is said to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can rephrase my question, Your Honour, if it's easier to proceed in another manner. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you are going to rephrase, you may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you've told us about the involvement that this person you knew as Toger had in the incident you've described today. Do you know whether any other soldiers of the FARK forces were mistreated in a similar way by Toger?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll object to those -- that question on two grounds: One, relevance; and the other is that it's leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You can respond, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same was suffered by a soldier of the 134th Brigade in Isniq. Toger had beaten him, had stripped him of his clothes. This was a young man from Drenoc. His name was Bujar. I can't recall his surname now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How do you know this, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came and informed the commander. These cases with Toger did not stop. Even after the agreement had been reached, he continued with his gestures and his acts against the soldiers of the 134th Brigade. As far as I remember, he once came to the barracks to take Rexh Osaj to arrest him or to take him. And had Tahir Zemaj not intervened, that would have happened. He entered the barracks without any permission and he wanted to take Rexh Osaj with him. I don't know where he wanted to take him or what he wanted to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said "had Tahir Zemaj not intervened, that would have happened." What did Tahir Zemaj do when Toger came to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there the moment when this happened. But when I went to the barracks later on, Rexh Osaj informed me that Toger had gone to the barracks, wanted to take Rexh Osaj with him, and Tahir Zemaj had intervened. And Toger had been in one room at the time, unarmed, and then later they had talked and released him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why it is that Toger came looking for Rexh Osaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You may respond, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rexh Osaj, during the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, the question was: Do you know why it is that Toger came looking for Rexh Osaj? Your answer is going to be "Yes, I know" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us why, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After Gllogjan had fallen into Serb hands, Rexh Osaj had gone to Irzniq, to the makeshift hospital in Irzniq, to retrieve some of the medication or other medical equipment that was there, IV drips and other things, whatever could be rescued from the hospital. And then he had gone back to the barracks, and Toger had come there later and asked him why he had been there, and accused him that, You have come to spy on us, to find out where our bases are. And so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, other than those incidents that you have described now, are you aware of any other incidents involving Toger where FARK soldiers were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember at this precise time. There was another incident I just remembered --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this a FARK incident?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... testifies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my recollection, there was a young man, a soldier of the 134th Brigade, he told us about his father who had been in an -- involved in an incident in Irzniq. His father was in a car when Toger had tried to stop him and he had not stopped right where Toger had told him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the question was related to FARK. This is not anything to do with FARK, although the soldier who's relating the incident may have been a FARK soldier. It's not a FARK incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we -- is this witness limited to testifying on FARK incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question that was -- the question that was asked related to FARK incidents. At page 78, line 18: "Sir, other than those incidents that you have described now, are you aware of any other incidents involving Toger where FARK soldiers were mistreated?" And since that is the question that was asked, the answer that was given does not respond to the question that was asked. It is non-responsive and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, just before Madam Kravetz responds --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can she deal with one thing at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I can rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can rephrase your question, okay. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps I should wait to see how Ms. Kravetz rephrases her question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, other than those incidents that you've described involving FARK soldiers, are you aware of any other incidents involving the person you knew as Toger where persons were mistreated? And by that I mean civilians or other soldiers were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that does engage the question that I would -- wanted to raise. Your Honours have ruled this witness's testimony admissible pro tem solely on the basis that it relates to a pleaded allegation in the JCE concerning the exclusion of FARK. Defence objected to the relevance of this witness's testimony to the counts which are in issue in the re-trial. The Prosecution responded: Well, we've chosen and are bound by the pleading of the JCE as originally before the first trial, which included an allegation concerning a joint enterprise to exclude FARK from Kosovo. And on that basis the Trial Chamber determined that this evidence was admissible. Anything travelling beyond that, which is apparently what the last question seeks to do, in our submission, goes beyond the terms of that ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is your submission, Mr. Emmerson, that the pleaded JCE is limited to the exclusion of FARK?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This -- I've got the decision in front of me. This decision of Your Honours on the admissibility of evidence was on the 23rd of August, 2011, at paragraph 51 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for reading slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Indicates that the suggested evidence related to a clash between the KLA and FARK and continues that it was relevant to allegations concerning the acts and conduct as alleged in the joint criminal enterprise in the indictment. Well, there's obviously some debate to be had in due course about whether FARK has anything remotely to do with the charges that the Tribunal is trying. But be that as it may, evidence that is beyond that, which the -- this witness was called to testify about, namely, the clashes between FARK and the KLA and upon which the Trial Chamber has determined his evidence is admissible, in our submission, travels beyond the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you've just read from the decision, and I didn't hear, from your reading, that the JCE in this case is limited to FARK or to the exclusion of FARK. And that's the question I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, clearly that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- so --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Indeed, the exclusion of FARK, in our submission, has nothing remotely to do with the JCE that is, in fact, being tried at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now we are probably talking at cross-purposes. My question to you is: Is it your submission that the JCE in this case is limited to the exclusion of FARK?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then you read me the decision of the Trial Chamber. What you read still hasn't answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, no, I mean, I think, Your Honour, that is the answer to the question. Of course it's not confined to the exclusion of FARK. The JCE is pleaded more broadly than that as in the original trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But, as the Trial Chamber is well aware, the issue for this re-trial is the JCE insofar as it applied to the commission of six crimes at Jabllanice. But it still retains an allegation concerning the FARK-KLA conflict. That is what this witness's evidence has been admitted as being relevant to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This witness is not -- are you saying this witness has been called here to come and testify only about FARK?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the way I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just if I could have a moment of indulgence just to find my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to repeat my last question to you. I asked you if other than those incidents that you've described involving FARK soldiers are you aware of any other incidents involving the person you knew as Toger where persons were mistreated?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to object to that because it goes outside of not only the purpose that this witness has been called for - and I understand your position, Judge - but it also does not tie into the JCE as pled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the JCE as pled, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The JCE as pled is as follows: The common criminal purpose of the JCE was to consolidate the total control of the KLA over the Dukagjin Operational Zone by the unlawful removal and mistreatment of Serb civilians and by the mistreatment of Kosovar Albanian and Kosovar Roma/Egyptian civilians and other civilians who were or perceived to have been collaborators with the Serbian forces or otherwise not supporting the KLA. And it is that to what I'm referring to right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I must rule you out of order, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, unless there's a causal connection between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Causal connection --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- between -- excuse me. Unless there's a causal connection between, as the Prosecution asserts, mistreatment and the purpose of that mistreatment as alleged in the indictment, it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you have told us that the purpose of the JCE was to consolidate control within that area and by -- and that was done by mistreatment of Serb civilians and by the mistreatment of Kosovar Albanian, Kosovar Roma/Egyptian civilians. I think we are dealing here with maybe someone who was a civilian -- or I don't know what the status of this person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But it's not only that, Your Honour. There is a relationship between the mistreatment of those civilians and the purpose of that mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And until there's a nexus established between those two, which is mistreatment and the purpose of that mistreatment, it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we will hear what the purpose was if this witness can be allowed to answer questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But that's a different issue, Your Honour, because the question that's being put forth is not that but, rather: Do you know of any mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will be told why was that mistreatment exercised or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we have yet to be told that at all with regard to any witness. I mean with regard to any of this gentleman's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember my question or should I put it to you again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I had -- and I'm just going to rephrase it just not to waste time looking for my question. I had asked you, sir, whether other than for the incidents you've described involving FARK soldiers are you aware of any other instances involving the person you knew as Toger where persons were mistreated? And by "persons," I mean both civilian and soldiers. Are you aware of any other incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In Irzniq - and this information I got from the son of the person in question who was travelling in his car - Toger ordered him to stop but he was not able to stop immediately at the place where Toger had asked him. The car had stopped a few metres further. Toger went there up to the car and directed the pistol to him and told him, You know, when I tell you to stop you have to stop where I tell you and not a few metres further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did Toger do anything? Or what happened after he said these -- do you know what happened after he said these words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You told us that Toger went up to the car and directed the pistol at this person and told him, You know, when I tell you to stop you have to stop where I tell you, not a few metres further. Do you know what happened after he said these words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before he said those words, he had shot him in the foot and then he told him, You have to stop where I tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who was this person that was shot at by Toger on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Adem Lokaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question as phrased. He -- she can ask the question: Who was he told was shot, but that assumes that he was shot. There is an assumption being made here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think it -- the witness has already indicated that the person was shot, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He has told -- he has indicated that what the objection is, that the witness has been -- was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- told us that he was told that the person had been shot. But now you are stating it as a fact, that: Who was this person who was shot? Now, you've got to say: Who was this person who you were told was shot? That's what you are being asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can put the question again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, who was this person you were told was shot by Toger on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Adem Lokaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who was he, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the father of a young man who was a member of the 134th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, did you eventually leave Kosovo in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left because I wanted to be safe and not be killed. Because many things had happened and I thought maybe one day I could be killed and nobody would know whether I would be killed by Albanians or by Serbs. I had Commander Zemaj and he authorised me to leave Kosovo, and that's what I did. There were other stronger reasons. When we were in Ulqin when -- where we heard that five people had been killed, all of them were members of the 134th Brigade or later as it was known, the Mergimi Brigade. And it was said that these people had been taken by Toger and killed, and it was for that reason that I then left Montenegro as well and set off for Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, I interpose an objection with regard to this particular rumour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was about to ask the witness for the source of this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who did you hear this from, this incident involving the killing of five people, members of the 134th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage I have no further questions for this witness. I would like to ask, given that there are persons present in the public gallery, that if my colleagues are going to pose any questions regarding the incident that the witness has described, that that be done in private session for the same reasons that I led the witness through that evidence in private session. I would also ask that if reference is going to be made to a protected witness who testified in the previous case in relation to the same incident, that that -- those questions be put to the witness in private session, again for purposes of protecting the identity of that witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And also when you see and there's an occasion where the need arises, you can rise and tell us when, because we won't know. Any cross-examination, Mr. Emmerson? We have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well I'll make a start, but I shall be some time into tomorrow with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 77, I'm going to ask you some questions about FARK generally. But before I do, can I just clarify one matter with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this is as much for Your Honours' assistance as for the witness's at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is no dispute that there was a confrontation in Gllogjan on the 4th of July in which there was physical confrontation and in which shots were fired. And it's the detail and the context of that incident that I want to ask some questions about. Witness 77, first of all, I just want to get the picture clear as far as the entry of FARK into Kosovo is concerned. So that the Trial Chamber understands, FARK -- the FARK brigades consists of, you told us, about 200 men and 25 officers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, there's obviously an automatic process by which my microphone is turned off and the witness is answering. I can see the Registrar trying to assist me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you can please switch off the microphone every time the witness is answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The FARK forces considered themselves to be acting with the authority of the Kosovar Albanian government in exile; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't claim to. They acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the self-styled so-called government in exile, did that government have a mandate as a result of elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Where and when were those elections held, Witness 77?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kosova. I don't remember when.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And were they organised with a universal right to vote so that all Kosovar Albanians had an opportunity to choose their government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the end result was a force of about 225 men, you've told us. And did you, those of you who entered Kosovo at the end of June, did you think you could defeat the Serbs with about 225 men on your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could have defeated the Serbs even without weapons if the people were what they should be, to fight for their country and not for the past. And we were not as many as you mentioned, but we had soldiers being drilled in Papaj [as interpreted], and they were coming to Kosova every day. We were not employing soldiers who had not the least knowledge of fighting and of using weapons, people who joined the fighting without knowing how to fire a shot. That's why the Kosovo government was there, to organise the people, to organise the youth, to train them how to fight, and to have a single command and not to have as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll come in a few moments to start asking you some questions about the way in which FARK entered and the conflict between the two, but based on your own personal experience are you suggesting that the FARK forces that entered Kosovo at the end of June/beginning of July were professional in training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So I take it that you yourself had had some training, had you, in military matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, you told us a minute ago the forces were professional. You now tell us you had had no military training. Had any of the soldiers had military training; and if so, what percentage, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already explained that the 25 officers were professional soldiers. But I meant the army in general. I meant the young people who were being trained on how to use weapons, how to dismantle the weapons, how to defend yourself, when to fire, how many munition you should have. Elementary things. As for the professionals, I referred only to the officers, the army officers, not to the army in general, to the rank-and-file soldiers who at least knew how to fire a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what was your rank when you entered Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was simple soldier, a voluntary soldier. I wanted simply to help my people. I didn't have any ranks, and I was not interested in anything to do with ranking.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Given that you've told us that the 25 officers were professional, presumably they taught you - you personally - at least the basics of the laws of war, did they, that you could kill combatants but not kill civilians? Did they teach you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't teach us that, but the commander of the brigade kept saying always: Whatever happens, take it easy because we are not here to fight against the Albanians but the Serb forces. And whatever may happen, for the moment we should disregard it because we don't want to engage in fratricide. This is what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Leaving fratricide apart for a moment: When you personally entered Kosovo, did you know that you were lawfully allowed to shoot combatants but that you were not lawfully allowed to shoot non-combatants, or civilians? Did you know that difference, you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So on the 4th of July, the day that this confrontation occurred, let's just be clear --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Witness 77, you've given some answers in private session about a particular incident and I'm not asking you about the details of that incident. But you've just confirmed to us on the record in private session that on the day in question you were, as were your colleagues, active combatants on active service. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, returning to the entry of the FARK forces into Kosovo at the -- that in the latter part of June, I want to put some specific dates to you, bearing in mind of course that this Tribunal has heard detailed evidence from witnesses, including a senior FARK officer, about the process by which FARK forces came to enter Kosovo. And I want to suggest to you that after your entry across the border from Albania there were, in fact, three meetings in the Jasiq/Junik area between the commanders of your force and the commanders of the Kosovo Liberation Army who were already on the ground inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that one was on the 25th of June in Jasiq; that a second took place on the 26th of June in Jasiq and then in Junik, and that it was on that occasion that Mr. Haradinaj was present; and that a third took place on the 30th of June in Junik. Is that possibly right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You knew, didn't you, that there was a significant and principled difference of opinion between your commander, Tahir Zemaj, and the commanders who were already operating on the ground inside Kosovo about deployment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that there was a dispute between the commanders of FARK, including Tahir Zemaj, and the commanders of the KLA inside Kosovo, including Mr. Haradinaj and Mr. Maloku, about the deployment of FARK soldiers. And I can put it a bit more specifically. Those who were already organised on the ground inside Kosovo wanted the FARK brigades to be distributed amongst the already organising village defence units, whereas the FARK commanders under Zemaj considered it essential that all of the 225 FARK officers remain together and in one place. That was the dispute, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I see the time. I'm not sure what point Your Honours wish to rise, but to take this line further I'm going to need to go into private session to identify the senior commander who testified at the previous trial and to put to this witness the evidence that that individual gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it does seem, of course, that you are not going to be able to do that within the time left for the day, so we might have to stop at this stage if it is convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's convenient for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll do that. May the Chamber please move into closed session. And as we do that, before we are finally into closed session, I just want to warn the witness, Mr. Registrar, to say that: Sir, we are not done with your testimony. You will come back here tomorrow. But we want to say to you that remember you are on the witness-stand; you may not talk to anybody about this case until you have been finally excused from further testifying. Especially, you may not talk to these people from the Prosecution. Thank you so much. Yes, we may move into closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of September, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
